text_blocks.snippet: Flexor tendon injuries usually require surgical repair, followed by a period of immobilization and hand therapy. The specific treatment plan depends on the severity and location of the injury, as well as the time elapsed since the injury. Early surgical intervention is often favored to optimize outcomes.
snippet_highlighted_words: surgical repair, followed by a period of immobilization and hand therapy

list.title: Timing:
list.snippet: Surgery is typically performed within 7-10 days of the injury, but immediate surgery may be necessary if there is restricted blood flow.

list.title: Procedure:
list.snippet: The surgeon reconnects the torn or cut tendon ends using sutures. The type of suture material and technique may vary.

list.title: Post-Surgery:
list.snippet: A splint or cast is applied to protect the repair and keep the tendon in a flexed position to reduce tension.

list.title: Hand Therapy:
list.snippet: A certified hand therapist plays a crucial role in recovery, guiding patients through exercises to improve motion and strength.

list.title: Splinting:
list.snippet: The initial splint may be replaced with a lighter, more flexible splint, allowing for protected movement.

list.title: Exercises:
list.snippet: Therapy involves gentle, controlled movements to prevent stiffness and adhesions, gradually increasing range of motion and strength.

list.title: Duration:
list.snippet: Recovery can take several months, with full strength returning in about three months and improved movement potentially continuing for up to six months.

list.title: Partial Lacerations:
list.snippet: If the injury involves less than 50% of the tendon, surgery may not be necessary. In such cases, the frayed ends may be trimmed, and immediate active movement may be encouraged to prevent adhesions.

list.title: Conservative Management:
list.snippet: For strained flexor tendons, rest, anti-inflammatory medications, and hand physiotherapy may be sufficient.
Follow Instructions: Following the surgeon's and therapist's instructions carefully is crucial for a successful outcome.
Potential Complications: Stiffness, tendon rupture, and impaired function can occur despite treatment.
Long-Term Goals: The long-term goal is to regain full hand function and prevent re-injury.

text_blocks.snippet: An FDS (flexor digitorum superficialis) injury refers to damage to the tendon that helps bend the fingers at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. These injuries can range from minor tears to complete ruptures and are often caused by cuts, sports injuries, or forceful movements. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and an inability to bend the finger at the PIP joint. Treatment typically involves surgery for complete tears, followed by hand therapy to restore function.
snippet_highlighted_words: damage to the tendon that helps bend the fingers at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint

list.title: FDS vs. FDP:
list.snippet: The FDS (flexor digitorum superficialis) tendon is one of two flexor tendons in each finger. The other is the FDP (flexor digitorum profundus), which flexes the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint.

list.title: Mechanism of Injury:
list.snippet: FDS injuries often occur when the finger is forcefully extended while actively flexing, like during a fall or while catching a ball.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Besides pain and swelling, patients may experience a catching sensation or clicking with finger movement, or an inability to fully bend the finger.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: A physical exam by a hand surgeon is crucial. The surgeon will assess the range of motion, strength, and sensation in the affected finger, and may use imaging like X-rays or MRI to further evaluate the injury.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Minor tears may heal with conservative treatment like splinting and therapy, but complete tears usually require surgical repair.

list.title: Rehabilitation:
list.snippet: Hand therapy is essential for regaining strength and range of motion after surgery, with specific protocols tailored to the injury and repair.
Lacerations: Cuts to the palm side of the hand or fingers can sever the FDS tendon.
Avulsions: The tendon can be pulled away from its attachment to the bone, either partially or completely.
Ruptures: The tendon can rupture due to trauma or overuse.
Jersey Finger: A specific type of avulsion injury where the FDP tendon is pulled away from its attachment, sometimes with an associated FDS injury.
Stiffness: Adhesions (scar tissue) can form around the tendon, limiting movement.
Rupture: The repaired tendon can rupture during rehabilitation if the repair is not strong enough or if the therapy is too aggressive.
Nerve or Blood Vessel Damage: Injuries to the median nerve or blood vessels can occur, causing numbness, tingling, or impaired blood flow.
